blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Prehistoric India covers the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, and Neolithic ages marked by stone tool evolution and site settlements.
The Indus Valley Civilization featured advanced town planning, unique scripts, and extensive trade networks.
The Vedic transition from Early to Later periods witnessed significant shifts in socio-political structure and religion.

Prehistory refers to the long period of human existence before the invention of writing. Since no written records were maintained, historians reconstruct this era using archaeological sources such as stone tools, pottery, fossils, bones, cave paintings, and human remains. This phase is popularly called the Stone Age because early humans primarily used stone to manufacture tools for survival.

Early humans lived a primitive life and depended entirely on nature. Over time, humans gradually learned to make tools, control fire, domesticate animals, and cultivate crops. These developments laid the foundation of civilization.

blocks.content: The Stone Age represents the earliest stage of human cultural development. Based on technological progress and lifestyle, it is divided into three major phases.
Duration: Approximately 2.5 million years ago – 10,000 BCE
Humans were nomadic and moved from place to place in search of food.
They lived in caves, rock shelters, and river valleys.
Their main occupation was hunting animals and gathering wild fruits and roots.
They had no knowledge of agriculture or pottery.
Tools were made of rough and unpolished stones.
The greatest achievement of this period was the discovery of fire, which provided warmth, protection, and cooked food.

The Indus Valley Civilization (IVC), also known as the Harappan Civilization, was one of the earliest urban civilizations in the world. It flourished around 2500 BCE – 1750 BCE and belonged to the Bronze Age. It represents the first urbanization in the Indian subcontinent.
The civilization developed mainly in the north-western regions of South Asia and is known for its advanced town planning, drainage system, trade networks, and craftsmanship.
The term 'Indus Valley Civilization' was first used by John Marshall.
Major rivers associated with the civilization include the Indus, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Ghaggar-Hakra.
The Harappan cities demonstrate remarkable urban planning. Cities were carefully laid out showing a high degree of civic sense.
Cities followed a grid pattern with roads intersecting at right angles.
Division of city into Citadel (upper town) and Lower Town.
Economy was based on agriculture, trade, and crafts.
Wheat and barley were main crops.
Harappans were the first to grow cotton.
Extensive internal and external trade existed.

No coins found — barter system was used.
Unicorn was the most common animal.

People wore cotton and woolen clothes.
Ornaments were made of gold, silver, and beads.
First urban civilization in India – Indus Valley Civilization

The Vedic Period marks an important phase in ancient Indian history. It is named after the Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of India. The Aryans, who composed the Vedas, settled in India during this period.

The Vedic Age is broadly divided into two phases: Early Vedic Period (Rig Vedic Age) and Later Vedic Period. This era witnessed significant developments in society, economy, religion, and political organization.
The Early Vedic Period is primarily known through the Rig Veda, the oldest of the four Vedas. The Aryans initially settled in the north-western region of India.
The basic political unit was the 'Jana' (tribe).
The tribe was headed by a king called 'Rajan'.
The king was not absolute and was assisted by tribal assemblies.
Important assemblies included Sabha (council of elders) and Samiti (general assembly).
Cattle rearing was the main occupation.
Wealth was measured in terms of cows.
Trade was conducted through barter system.
Important gods: Indra (rain & war), Agni (fire), Varuna (water), Surya (sun).
No temples or idol worship existed.
The Later Vedic Period saw expansion of Aryans towards the Gangetic plains. This period experienced major transformations in political structure, economy, and social organization.
King's power increased and became hereditary.
Emergence of powerful states called Mahajanapadas.
Varna system became rigid and birth-based.
Use of iron tools improved farming.
Trade expanded and coins such as 'Nishka' appeared.
Concepts like Karma and Rebirth developed.

The 6th century BCE is known as the Age of Religious Revolution in India. Later Vedic society had become highly ritualistic, expensive sacrifices were common, and the Varna system had turned rigid. This led to dissatisfaction among common people. As a result, new religions such as Buddhism and Jainism emerged which emphasized ethical conduct, non‑violence and equality.
At the same time, political consolidation resulted in the rise of large territorial states known as Mahajanapadas.
The word Mahajanapada means 'Great Kingdom'. Around the 6th century BCE, sixteen powerful states dominated northern India.
Use of iron tools improved agriculture.

After the rise of Mahajanapadas, Magadha emerged as the most powerful kingdom. This ultimately led to the establishment of the Mauryan Empire, the first empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent. Following the decline of the Mauryas, several smaller kingdoms arose before the Guptas established another great empire.

After the decline of the Gupta Empire around the 6th century CE, northern and southern India witnessed the rise of several regional kingdoms. This period is known as the Early Medieval Period. Political unity disappeared, but it was also a time of major developments in temple architecture, regional cultures, literature, and trade.
The most important dynasties of this era include Harsha’s empire in North India and powerful southern kingdoms such as the Chalukyas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas, and Palas.
Harsha was one of the most prominent rulers of post-Gupta northern India. After the death of his brother Rajyavardhana, Harsha ascended the throne at a young age and gradually built a vast empire.

The Delhi Sultanate refers to the period when several Muslim dynasties ruled large parts of India from Delhi. It began with the establishment of the Slave Dynasty in 1206 and ended with the defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur in the First Battle of Panipat (1526), leading to the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
There were FIVE dynasties that ruled during the Delhi Sultanate period.

The Mughal Empire was one of the greatest empires in Indian history. Founded by Babur in 1526 after the First Battle of Panipat, the empire brought political unity, administrative reforms, economic prosperity, and architectural brilliance. The Mughal period is often considered a high point of cultural synthesis in India.

The discovery of sea routes to India led to the arrival of European trading companies. Their primary objective was trade, especially in spices, textiles, and precious goods. Over time, commercial rivalry turned into political control, ultimately leading to British dominance in India.
Decline Reasons: Corruption, competition from other Europeans, and weak administration.
